title: Adult Choking First Aid Protocol
content:
1. Verify if the person can speak, cough, or breathe. If they can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing.
2. If unable to breathe or speak, give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
3. If back blows fail, stand behind them, place a fist just above the navel, grasp with your other hand, and perform up to 5 quick inward and upward abdominal thrusts.
4. Alternate between 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the airway is clear.
5. If the person becomes unresponsive, lower them to the ground and start CPR immediately while calling 112.
source_name: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) First Aid Guidelines

title: Severe Bleeding First Aid Protocol
content:
1. Ensure personal safety and, if available, wear protective gloves.
2. Apply firm, direct pressure on the wound using a clean cloth, sterile dressing, or your hands.
3. Maintain continuous direct pressure without removing the cloth. If blood soaks through, add another layer on top.
4. Keep the injured person calm and lying down to prevent shock.
5. If bleeding is life-threatening on a limb and direct pressure fails, apply a commercial tourniquet 2-3 inches above the wound (never over a joint) and record the time applied.
6. Keep the person warm while awaiting emergency services.
source_name: American Red Cross First Aid / Stop The Bleed Guidelines

title: Thermal Burns First Aid Protocol
content:
1. Remove the heat source immediately and ensure the area is safe.
2. Cool the burn under cool, gently running tap water for at least 10 to 20 minutes. Do NOT use ice, iced water, or greasy substances like butter or toothpaste.
3. Gently remove jewelry, rings, or tight items near the burned area before swelling occurs. Do NOT pull away clothing stuck to the burn.
4. Loosely cover the burn with clean, non-stick plastic wrap (cling film) or a clean, dry lint-free cloth.
5. Do NOT burst any blisters.
6. Seek immediate medical attention or call 112 if the burn is large, on face/hands/joints, or affects a child.
source_name: World Health Organization (WHO) Burn Prevention and Management

title: Unconscious Person First Aid Protocol
content:
1. Check for danger in the surroundings before approaching.
2. Gently tap the person's shoulders and ask loudly: 'Are you okay?'.
3. If no response, check for normal breathing by tilting the head back, lifting the chin, and looking/listening/feeling for chest movement for no more than 10 seconds.
4. If the person is breathing normally, place them in the recovery position (on their side with airway open) and monitor them continuously.
5. If the person is NOT breathing or only gasping, immediately call 112 and begin CPR (30 chest compressions at 100-120 bpm, followed by 2 rescue breaths if trained, or hands-only CPR).
source_name: British Red Cross / Resuscitation Council UK

title: Breathing Emergency / Asthma Attack Protocol
content:
1. Help the person sit upright in a comfortable position and loosen tight clothing around the neck. Do NOT lay them flat.
2. Reassure the person to help keep them calm.
3. Help them use their reliever inhaler (usually blue) with a spacer if available: give 1 puff every 30-60 seconds up to 10 puffs.
4. If symptoms do not improve after 10 puffs, if the person cannot speak in sentences, or if condition worsens, call 112 immediately.
5. Keep monitoring breathing until emergency help arrives.
source_name: Asthma + Lung UK Emergency First Aid Guidelines

title: General Adult CPR Protocol (Cardiac Arrest)
content:
1. Confirm the scene is safe and check for responsiveness and normal breathing.
2. Call 112 immediately or instruct a bystander to call and fetch an AED (defibrillator) if available.
3. Position your hands in the center of the chest.
4. Push hard and fast: compress at a depth of 5 to 6 cm (2 inches) at a rate of 100 to 120 beats per minute (e.g. to the beat of 'Stayin' Alive').
5. Allow full chest recoil between compressions.
6. Continue continuous chest compressions until emergency medical personnel take over or an AED is ready to analyze.
source_name: American Heart Association (AHA) CPR & ECC Guidelines

title: Seizure & Convulsions First Aid Protocol
content:
1. Stay calm and stay with the person. Note the time the seizure started.
2. Gently ease the person to the floor and place something soft under their head.
3. Clear the area of hard, sharp, or dangerous objects to prevent injury.
4. Turn the person gently onto one side (recovery position) to keep the airway clear.
5. Do NOT put anything in their mouth (they cannot swallow their tongue) and do NOT hold them down or restrain their movements.
6. Call 112 immediately if the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes, if another seizure follows immediately, if the person is pregnant or injured, or if they do not regain consciousness.
source_name: CDC & Epilepsy Foundation First Aid for Seizures

title: Suspected Stroke (F.A.S.T.) Protocol
content:
1. Check for F.A.S.T. warning signs:
   - F (Face): Ask them to smile. Does one side of the face droop?
   - A (Arms): Ask them to raise both arms. Does one arm drift downward?
   - S (Speech): Ask them to repeat a simple sentence. Is their speech slurred or strange?
   - T (Time): If you observe ANY of these signs, call 112 immediately!
2. Keep the person calm, comfortable, and resting with head and shoulders slightly elevated.
3. Note the exact time symptoms first began (crucial for hospital treatment).
4. Do NOT give them anything to eat or drink (including aspirin or water) due to choking risk.
5. If the person becomes unresponsive or stops normal breathing, begin CPR immediately.
source_name: American Stroke Association / American Heart Association

title: Severe Allergic Reaction / Anaphylaxis Protocol
content:
1. Call 112 immediately—anaphylaxis is a life-threatening medical emergency.
2. If the person has an auto-injector (EpiPen / epinephrine), help them use it immediately: press firmly into outer mid-thigh until it clicks, hold for 3-5 seconds, then massage area.
3. Have the person lie flat with legs elevated. If breathing is difficult, allow them to sit upright. Do NOT stand or walk them around.
4. If symptoms do not improve or return after 5 to 10 minutes and emergency services have not arrived, administer a second epinephrine dose if available.
5. Stay with the person continuously and monitor breathing until emergency medical help takes over.
source_name: American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology (AAAAI) / Red Cross

title: Head Injury, Concussion & Severe Headache First Aid
content:
1. Have the injured person sit or lie down comfortably and keep their head and neck still.
2. If there is external bleeding, apply gentle, direct pressure with a clean cloth. (Do NOT press forcefully if you suspect a skull fracture).
3. Apply a cold compress or cloth-wrapped ice pack to the painful area to reduce swelling.
4. Keep the person quiet and resting in a dimly lit, quiet room. Do NOT give aspirin or ibuprofen immediately if trauma or bleeding is suspected.
5. Call 112 immediately if there is: sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache, loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, confusion, slurred speech, clear fluid draining from nose or ears, or unequal pupils.
source_name: American Red Cross & CDC Heads Up Guidelines

title: Fever Assessment & Red-Flag Triage Guidelines
content:
1. Ensure the person stays hydrated with small, frequent sips of water or oral rehydration fluids. Do NOT use ice baths or cold sponge baths.
2. Dress the person in lightweight, breathable clothing and keep the room at a comfortable temperature.
3. Rest and monitor temperature using a reliable thermometer.
4. Warning Signs for Urgent Medical Assessment:
   - Infants under 3 months with temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher.
   - Fever lasting longer than 3 consecutive days.
   - Stiff neck, new unexplained rash, photophobia (light sensitivity), or persistent vomiting.
5. CALL 112 IMMEDIATELY if fever is accompanied by: difficulty breathing, blue/pale skin or lips, confusion, lethargy/unresponsiveness, or a seizure.
source_name: CDC & NHS Clinical Guidelines on Fever in Adults and Children
